nodes.label: Sack of Antwerp
nodes.full: Spanish troops sack Antwerp in 1576 and its sugar trade collapses.

nodes.label: Fujian sugar goes north
nodes.full: Wang Shimao lists Quanzhou and Zhangzhou cane sugar among Fujian goods shipped north.

nodes.label: Antwerp’s refineries
nodes.full: Antwerp has 19 sugar refineries by 1550, more than any other city.

nodes.label: Dutch refineries
nodes.full: Refineries in the northern Netherlands grow from 3–4 in 1595 to over 60 in 1661.

nodes.label: United Provinces
nodes.full: The war of 1572–85 makes Amsterdam Europe’s commercial centre and its sugar refiner.

nodes.label: Iberian Union
nodes.full: Philip II takes the Portuguese crown in 1580.

nodes.label: Dutch war in Brazil
nodes.full: The Dutch take Recife in 1630 and hold the sugar Nordeste for 24 years.

nodes.label: Dutch buy Chinese sugar
nodes.full: The Dutch company’s orders for Chinese sugar reach over 4 million lb in 1637.

nodes.label: Ballast sugar from Banten
nodes.full: Dutch ships carry China sugar from Banten in 1606–07.

nodes.label: Dutch Taiwan sugar
nodes.full: Taiwan exports 2.2 million lb of sugar in 1658, 780,000 of it to Japan.

nodes.label: Macao–Nagasaki sugar
nodes.full: Portuguese ships carry Chinese silk and sugar to Japan, 1600–39.

nodes.label: Portuguese excluded
nodes.full: The shogun excludes the Portuguese from Japan in 1639.

nodes.label: Brazilian engenhos
nodes.full: Brazil’s engenhos grow from the coast in 1520 to 66 in Pernambuco and 36 in Bahia by 1583.

nodes.label: Brazil supplies Europe
nodes.full: By 1625 Portugal supplies nearly all of Europe with Brazilian sugar.

nodes.label: Duty at Lisbon
nodes.full: Brazilian sugar pays duty at the Lisbon custom house by 1526.

nodes.label: Manuel’s charter
nodes.full: King Manuel’s 1516 charter asks for a sugar master in Brazil.

nodes.label: Three-roller mill
nodes.full: Brazil’s three-roller mill is adopted c.1608–12; its inventor is disputed.

nodes.label: Santo Domingo’s mill
nodes.full: Canary engineers build a two-roller mill at Santo Domingo c.1515.

nodes.label: Santo Domingo’s mills
nodes.full: Santo Domingo has 34 mills by the 1530s and estates of 150–200 enslaved people by 1568.

nodes.label: Aid to Santo Domingo
nodes.full: The Crown and Hieronymite fathers lend revenues to the island’s planters.

nodes.label: First Africans in Santo Domingo
nodes.full: Enslaved Africans are imported before 1503.

nodes.label: Taíno collapse
nodes.full: 80–90% of the islands’ indigenous people die within a century.

nodes.label: São Tomé
nodes.full: São Tomé’s sugar and its turn to slave-trading.

nodes.label: Portuguese slave trade
nodes.full: Portuguese ships carry about 264,000 Africans between 1519 and 1600.

nodes.label: Amador’s revolt
nodes.full: A revolt of enslaved people on São Tomé in 1595, whose evidence is disputed.

nodes.label: Claying in China
nodes.full: Claying whitens sugar in Ming China, c.1522–66.

nodes.label: Hernández’s hen
nodes.full: Hernández’s 1577 story of a hen whitening sugar.

nodes.label: Tiangong kaiwu
nodes.full: The 1637 Tiangong kaiwu shows a two-roller crusher and claying with mud water.

nodes.label: Song Yingxing
nodes.full: Song Yingxing opens his sugar section with ‘tastes that are sweet are generally desired by all’.

nodes.label: Animal candy recipe
nodes.full: The Tiangong kaiwu gives a recipe for animal-shaped candy.

nodes.label: Fuzhou banquet
nodes.full: Friars see sugar sculptures at the governor of Fuzhou’s banquet in 1575.

nodes.label: Hertford’s banquet
nodes.full: A sugar menagerie at an Earl of Hertford’s banquet for Elizabeth I.

nodes.label: Black teeth
nodes.full: Hentzner, Vaughan and Hart link sugar with rotten teeth, 1598–1633.

nodes.label: English privateers
nodes.full: English booty makes sugar cheaper in London than in Lisbon, a spy reports in 1591.

edges: Smith says Antwerp, Europe’s great refining city, was sacked in 1576 and its sugar trade collapsed; Mazumdar gives it 19 refineries by 1550.
Mazumdar: Antwerp’s pre-eminence was destroyed by the war and the division of the Netherlands (1572–85), and Amsterdam became the new centre.
Mazumdar links Amsterdam’s rise with its growth in sugar refining, from three or four refineries in 1595 to 29 in 1622.
Mazumdar: Portugal became a Spanish province in 1580, and the Dutch-Iberian rivalry became war in the Atlantic, reaching Brazil in 1624.
Mazumdar: the Dutch–Portuguese conflict in Brazil drove up the price of Brazilian sugar in Amsterdam, and so the Dutch company’s interest in Chinese sugar.
The company’s directors recommended regular sugar cargoes from Asia in 1616; the first Dutch sugar from Banten had gone in 1606–07.
Mazumdar: the apparent profits encouraged the Dutch to sponsor sugar in Taiwan and Batavia.
Dutch Taiwan sold 780,000 lb to Japan in 1658; by the 1630s Fujian traders and the Dutch had pushed the Portuguese out of the sugar trade there.
The Macao–Nagasaki trade collapsed in 1639 when the shogun excluded the Portuguese.
Mazumdar: the Dutch refineries’ raw sugar, about 45 million pounds, came from Portuguese-controlled Brazil.
Brazil’s engenhos, 66 in Pernambuco and 36 in Bahia by 1583, are what supplied nearly all of Europe by 1625.
Manuel’s 1516 charter asks for a sugar master, and the engenhos follow along the coast by 1520.
Brazilian sugar is paying duty at Lisbon by 1526, six years after Smith’s coastal engenhos of 1520.
Smith credits the engenhos with adopting the three-roller mill and the cauldron train in the early seventeenth century.
Mintz traces Santo Domingo’s two-roller mill to the design attributed to Pietro Speciale in 1449; Soares Pereira argues instead for Peru and 1608–12.
Mintz: the Canary engineers’ mill of about 1515 begins the industry that has 34 mills by the 1530s.
Mintz: Hieronymite loans and royal support helped planters build the mills, and civil servants owned and traded plantations.
Mintz: enslaved Africans were imported to work the royal mines and ‘others soon followed to power the sugar industry’; by 1568 estates had 150–200 enslaved people.
Smith and Mintz tie the shortage of indigenous labour, after the Taíno’s collapse, to the importing of African slaves.
Smith: São Tomé became the holding area and point of departure for slave ships bound for Brazil.
Smith: Brazil’s indigenous labour pool shrank and enslaved Africans, many first from São Tomé, replaced it.
Popular accounts say Amador’s 1595 revolt destroyed São Tomé’s mills, which is disputed.
Mazumdar sets Hernández’s hen story (1577) beside the Chinese roof-tile story as equally fanciful accounts of the discovery of claying.
Mazumdar: claying was introduced in the sixteenth century and standardised by 1637, when the Tiangong kaiwu describes it.
The Tiangong kaiwu illustrates both the two-roller crusher and claying; its sugar section opens with the remark that sweet tastes are universally desired.
The same work gives the recipe for animal-shaped candy.
Mazumdar compares the sugar sculptures at Fuzhou in 1575 with the sugar subtleties then fashionable in Europe.
Smith’s sugar-sculpture banquet for Elizabeth I of the 1590s and Hentzner’s 1598 remark on her black teeth belong to the same decade.
Fuzhou’s sugar sculptures of 1575 stand in Fujian, the province whose Quanzhou and Zhangzhou sugar Wang Shimao says was shipped north.
Mintz uses the 1591 report to show English interest in sugar before England had colonies; by 1625 Portugal supplies nearly all Europe.
